title: Make a cardboard telescope and find the Moon
description: The telescope in the picture is cardboard and patience. You can build a simple version from two tubes and two lenses — and its first and best target is hanging in the evening sky.

body.heading: Two lenses, two tubes
paragraphs: A refracting telescope is a long tube with a large lens at the front to gather light and a small eyepiece lens at the back to magnify. Slide one cardboard tube inside another so you can change the length — that sliding is how you focus.

Lens sets from a craft or science kit are the reliable route; magnifying glasses can work for a first experiment, though the image will be softer. Tape the front lens firmly so it cannot slip and scratch.

body.heading: First light: the Moon
paragraphs: Aim at the Moon on a clear evening — never at the Sun, which can permanently damage eyes even through a homemade tube. Slide the inner tube slowly until the Moon's edge sharpens, and the grey seas and bright highlands appear.

A homemade telescope will not rival a shop instrument, and that is its lesson: Galileo's telescope was cruder than yours, and it still showed him Jupiter's moons. The instrument matters less than the looking.

takeaway: Two lenses and sliding cardboard tubes make a working telescope: focus it on the Moon — never the Sun — and you are looking with better tools than Galileo had.
materials: Two cardboard tubes that slide inside each other
A telescope lens kit or two magnifying lenses
A clear evening with a visible Moon
supervision: An adult must supervise building and use, and must make the never-look-at-the-Sun rule absolute before the telescope is pointed anywhere.
safetyNotes: NEVER point any telescope or lens at the Sun — it can cause permanent eye damage instantly.
Use the telescope outdoors after dark with an adult present.
Store lenses covered so they do not gather dust or scratches.
